title: Buttercream basket weave
subtitle: How to pipe the classic interlocking pattern with a star or ribbon tip
excerpt: Basket weave uses two alternating rows of piped lines to build a woven grid on the sides of a cake. One row goes vertical, the next horizontal, each horizontal row bridging the gaps of the one above. It works with a star tip, a ribbon tip, or a plain round tip.
sourceNotes: Basket weave is a standard piping technique taught across confectionery training programmes and documented in decorating manuals from the mid-twentieth century onwards. The mechanics described here follow the pattern common to British sugarcraft instruction.

recipe.yieldDescription: Decoration for one 20 cm round cake
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Pipe the basket weave on a crumb-coated, chilled cake. Chill again for 20 minutes before serving to firm the buttercream.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin layer of buttercream applied before the final coat to seal in loose crumbs and give a smooth base for decoration.

content.text: Basket weave is an alternating grid of piped lines on the side of a cake. Two colours are optional but one reads clearly enough. The key is a firm buttercream at cool room temperature: too soft and the lines slump; too stiff and the bag tires your hand. Apply a
first and chill the cake for 20 minutes before piping.

A ribbon tip (number 47 or 48) gives the cleanest weave; one side is flat and the other ridged, so every line has a woven texture built in. A star tip (number 21 or 32) gives a more textured result. A plain round tip produces a tighter, slicker grid. All three work.
Place the cake on the turntable. Starting at the left of your working section, pipe a vertical line from top to bottom, pressing steady and even. Lift cleanly at the end.
Pipe a second vertical line the width of your tip to the right of the first. Leave a gap equal to the tip width between lines.
Continue across the section, alternating lines and gaps.
Pipe the first horizontal line at the top, passing over one vertical line and under the next (covering alternate lines). Each horizontal stroke bridges a gap.
Move down one tip width and pipe the next horizontal row, but start by passing under the first vertical line instead of over it. The pattern inverts at each row.
Continue down the cake, rotating the turntable as you complete each section. The end of each horizontal stroke butts up against the next vertical group.

A rope border or shell border along the top edge and the base hides the joins and ties the decoration together. Pipe these last when the basket weave is complete around the full circumference. Chill the finished cake for 15 minutes before it is moved.
Score a light grid on the chilled crumb coat with a toothpick as a guide before piping. The marks disappear under the final layer. This prevents the lines drifting diagonal as you rotate.
